bib.title: LazyLLM: Dynamic Token Pruning for Efficient Long Context LLM Inference

legacy_report:
SOURCE: LazyLLM: Dynamic Token Pruning for Efficient Long Context LLM Inference. Qichen Fu, Minsik Cho, Thomas Merth, Sachin Mehta, Mohammad Rastegari (Meta AI, work done at Apple), Mahyar Najibi (Apple). arXiv:2407.14057v1, 19 Jul 2024. Preprint.

COVERAGE: All 12 pages, about 40,500 of 40,545 chars. The extraction ended mid-reference (Xu et al. 2023, cut off). There is no appendix: the paper ends with the conclusion and references. I did not run figures.py. Figures 5, 6 and 7 are plots whose data did not extract, so I report only their text captions and takeaways.

CLAIMS (ranked)
- claim: Prefill (TTFT) is a large share of long-prompt generation time. For Llama 2 7B on LongBench, TTFT costs 21x one decoding step and about 23% of total generation time.
  number: 21x; 23%
  setup: Llama 2 7B, LongBench. Average prompt is 3376 tokens and average generation is 68 tokens.
  quote: "TTFT requires 21× the walltime of each subsequent decoding step, and accounts for approximately 23% of the total generation time on the LongBench benchmark"
  where: p.1; footnote 1 on p.1 for the average lengths

- claim: LazyLLM speeds up TTFT on multi-document QA with negligible accuracy loss.
  number: 2.34x TTFT (Llama 2), 2.65x (XGen); Llama 2 score 22.31 vs baseline 22.43
  setup: Llama 2 7B and XGen 7B, LongBench, A100 GPUs, no training, wall-clock, 5 warmup runs
  quote: "our method can offer 2.34× TTFT speedup in the multi-document question-answering task with negligible (≤ 1%) performance loss."
  where: p.7 (§5.2); Table 1, p.7

- claim: Pushing harder gives about 3x TTFT with up to 10% accuracy loss, while baselines degrade much more at similar speedup.
  number: 3.0x; ≤10% degradation
  setup: Llama 2 7B, multi-doc QA, varying pruning hyperparameters (Fig 5)
  quote: "LazyLLM can achieve 3.0× TTFT speedup in the multi-document question-answering task with ≤ 10% degradation in accuracy."
  where: p.7

- claim: Table 1 gives TTFT speedup and score per task (Llama 2 / XGen). Baseline score, then LazyLLM score and speedup.
  number: Single-doc QA 25.79 -> 25.59, 1.36x / 25.19 -> 25.00, 1.96x. Multi-doc QA 22.43 -> 22.31, 2.34x / 20.71 -> 20.68, 2.65x. Summarization 24.65 -> 24.75, 1.46x / 24.85 -> 24.74, 1.91x. Few-shot 62.90 -> 62.81, 2.19x / 56.40 -> 56.12, 3.42x. Synthetic 4.97 -> 4.98, 2.89x / 5.40 -> 5.66, 4.77x. Code 55.18 -> 53.30, 1.94x / 36.49 -> 36.47, 3.47x.
  setup: as above, macro-averaged scores per task category
  quote: "LazyLLM (Ours) 22.31 2.34 20.68 2.65" (multi-doc row); "LazyLLM (Ours) 53.30 1.94 36.47 3.47" (code row)
  where: Table 1, p.7
  note: Code completion on Llama 2 shows the largest accuracy drop, 55.18 to 53.30.

- claim: LazyLLM beats the baselines at similar speedup. Random token drop and static pruning lose far more accuracy. Prompt compression (LLMLingua-style, Li et al. 2023) makes TTFT slower than baseline because of its overhead.
  number: Prompt compression TTFT speedup 0.10x to 0.49x on Llama 2. Multi-doc QA score for compression is 8.42 vs 22.43 baseline.
  setup: Table 1, same models and tasks. Random drop is averaged over 5 runs. Static pruning prunes once using the attention of the first few layers during prefill.
  quote: "the actual TTFT of the “prompt compression” baseline is longer than the baseline."
  where: p.6; Table 1 p.7
  note: Static pruning also collapses on synthetic tasks (2.81 vs 4.97 baseline on Llama 2).

- claim: LazyLLM also speeds up overall generation, because some prompt tokens are never computed.
  number: Generation speedup 1.01x to 1.79x (Llama 2), 1.09x to 3.16x (XGen). Prompt tokens computed: 63.73% (synthetic, Llama 2) to 99.59% (summarization).
  setup: same setting as Table 1
  quote: "SYNTHETIC 63.73 40 .54 1 .79 3 .16"; "MULTI-DOCUMENT QA 63.94 69 .60 1 .56 1 .70"
  where: Table 2, p.8
  note: Summarization barely benefits (1.02x, 99.59% of tokens computed).

- claim: Pruning at later layers hurts less than pruning at earlier layers, and keeping fewer tokens lowers the score. This motivates progressive pruning, keeping more tokens early and fewer late.
  number: none; Fig 6 keep ratios are 10, 30, 50, 70 and 90% of tokens
  setup: single-shot pruning at one layer, Llama 2 7B and XGen 7B
  quote: "pruning at later transformer layers consistently yields better performance compared to pruning at earlier layers, suggesting that later layers are less sensitive to token pruning."
  where: p.8-9 (§5.4)

- claim: Attention of input tokens toward the next token is very sparse, so many prompt tokens are redundant.
  number: none
  setup: Llama 2 7B on LongBench (Fig 2)
  quote: "the attention scores of input tokens w.r.t. to the next token are very sparse, indicating that many tokens in the input prompt are redundant"
  where: p.2-3

- claim: Method. Each layer scores token i by the head-averaged attention from the last token. Tokens below the layer's top-k percentile are pruned and are absent from all later layers. Pruned tokens can be revived at later generation steps. Aux Cache stores their hidden states, so each token is computed at most once per layer and worst-case runtime is no slower than baseline.
  number: none
  setup: Eq. 1 is s_i^l = (1/H) Σ_h A^l_{h,i,N}. Percentile thresholding is used because score distributions vary by layer and task.
  quote: "The introduction of Aux Cache ensures that each token is computed at most once in every transformer layer, and ensures the worst runtime of LazyLLM is not slower than the baseline."
  where: p.4-6 (§3.2)
  note: The claim of reviving tokens being "crucial" rests on the comparison to static pruning in Table 1. There is no dedicated ablation.

- claim: Cumulative token usage over decoding steps stays below the baseline. The authors argue the model effectively drops tokens that do not affect output.
  number: none (Fig 7)
  setup: Llama 2 7B, 1000 random LongBench samples, per layer group (1-9, 10-19, 20-28, 29-32)
  quote: "Our analysis supports the hypothesis that many tokens are never selected by the model"
  where: p.9-10 (§5.5)

LIMITS
- Only 7B models (Llama 2 7B, XGen 7B) and only LongBench. No larger models, no other benchmarks, no batching or serving-system (vLLM) results.
- Timing is HuggingFace transformers on A100 with batch size not stated. The paper says only wall-clock with 5 warmup runs.
- Exact pruning schedule (which layers, which k percentiles) is not given in the text. Only the Fig 4 sketch with 30%/10%/30%/30% layer splits and "Prune 30% tokens" is shown. It is not stated whether Table 1 uses one setting per task.
- Speedup depends on the task. Summarization gets 1.46x and 1.02x overall, because it needs most tokens.
- The authors concede no limitations section. They only note that over-pruning causes information loss (§5.2).
- Code completion on Llama 2 shows the largest accuracy loss (55.18 to 53.30).
- Interaction with FlashAttention (which needs the full attention map for scoring) and with speculative decoding is not examined.
- The token-importance assumption (last-token attention in the prior layer) is not validated against alternatives.
- Dated: 2024 preprint, v1.

BUILDS ON
- Layer-wise early-exit and hidden-state evolution: Elhoushi et al., 2024 (LayerSkip). This inspired layer-wise pruning.
- Learned Token Pruning: Kim et al., 2022. Token pruning for classification: He et al., 2021 (Magic Pyramid); Anagnostidis et al., 2024.
- KV-cache reduction by attention importance: Zhang et al., 2024 (H2O); Li et al., 2024 (SnapKV); Adnan et al., 2024 (Keyformer); Nawrot et al., 2024. These need profiling of the first few tokens, so they do not reduce TTFT.
- Prompt compression: Li et al., 2023; Jiang et al., 2023 (LLMLingua); Xu et al., 2023. The random drop baseline follows Yao et al., 2022.
- Benchmark and models: Bai et al., 2023 (LongBench); Touvron et al., 2023 (Llama 2); Nijkamp et al., 2023 (XGen).
- Decoding-stage speedups: Leviathan et al., 2023 (speculative decoding); Medusa (Cai et al., 2024).
- Long-context architectures: Longformer (Beltagy 2020), Reformer (Kitaev 2020). FlashAttention (Dao 2022).

CODE: none in the paper. There is no pseudocode. The implementation is HuggingFace-based and no repo link is given.

FIGURES (captions read, not rendered)
- Fig 1, p.2: prefill vs decode stages, with TTFT at 21x a decode step and 23% of total time.
- Fig 2, p.3: attention sparsity per layer for Llama 2 7B, and the distribution of average attention. Evidence for the whole premise.
- Fig 3, p.4: standard vs LazyLLM token computation over iterations. Accumulated tokens computed are 13/14/15 for standard vs 4/6/7 for LazyLLM. Shows the mechanics fastest.
- Fig 4, p.5: framework with progressive layer-wise pruning, KV cache and Aux Cache.
- Fig 5, p.8: TTFT speedup vs relative score for the 6 tasks, Llama 2 7B, against the 4 baselines.
- Fig 6, p.9: score vs pruning layer index for keep ratios of 10 to 90%.
- Fig 7, p.9: cumulative % of prompt tokens computed per generation step, per layer group.

PROBLEMS: None serious. Figure data (plot values) did not extract, so Fig 5 and Fig 6 numbers are unavailable. The reference list is cut off at the last entry. No embedded instructions found in the PDF.
